title: Lesson 5: Overview of the Bible
description: A young king finds a lost book in God's house. This lesson gives you the map of the Bible: a library of 66 books where every shelf points to Jesus.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you saw that you are rooted in Jesus, and one of the deepest roots is the Word of God. The next three lessons belong together. This lesson gives you the map, the next takes you on the road trip through the Bible's one big story, and the third hands you the skill to dig into any passage on your own.

blocks.title: The Book Found in the Temple
blocks.text:
Josiah became king of Judah when he was only eight years old. The kings before him had filled the land with idols, and God's own house in Jerusalem had fallen into disrepair. When Josiah was a young man, he sent workers to repair the temple.

In the middle of the dust and the repairs, the high priest made a discovery:

"I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD." (2 Kings 22:8)

Think about that. God's Word had been lost, and not in some far-off country. It was lost inside the house of God. The people still went through the motions of religion, but no one was listening to what God had actually said.

The king's secretary read the scroll aloud, and as the words landed, the young king saw how far his people had drifted from the God who loved them. "When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes" (2 Kings 22:11). He humbled himself before the LORD, and God heard him.

Then Josiah gathered all the people, both small and great, and read the book in their hearing. He renewed the covenant and tore down the idols. Scripture remembers him this way: "Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might" (2 Kings 23:25).

One lost book, found and read, turned a whole nation back to God.

Many homes have a Bible the way the temple had that scroll: in the house, just not opened. If that is you, it is not a reason for shame. It is the reason for this lesson. Once you know how God's library is arranged, you can take His Word off the shelf with confidence.
Carry this one sentence through the lesson: God's Word is a library to open, not a book to lose on a shelf, and every shelf points to Jesus.
5.1 - What tends to keep the Bible on the shelf for you?
A Library, Not a Single Book

blocks.alt: A bookshelf displaying all 66 books of the Bible organized by section

blocks.text: The Bible is not a single book. It is a library of 66 books, written by about 40 authors across roughly 1,500 years. Among the writers are kings, shepherds, fishermen, a doctor, a tax collector, and prophets. And yet the whole library tells one unified story from beginning to end, as you will see in the next lesson.
That unity fits what the Bible says about where it came from:
All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
When you open the Bible, you are not reading someone's best guesses about life. You are reading words the living God intended for you to have.

Can a book copied by hand for centuries still be trusted? God preserved His Word through public reading, careful copying, and many manuscripts that scholars can compare. The Dead Sea Scrolls, copied before the time of Jesus, include a nearly complete copy of Isaiah, and they showed how carefully the Old Testament had been preserved. Most differences between copies are spelling, word order, or small copying slips. You are not building your life on a rumor that changed in the shadows. You are opening a Word God has carried faithfully through time.
Old Testament and New Testament

The library has two main parts. The word "testament" means covenant, a binding promise between God and His people. The 39 books of the Old Testament tell how God created the world, chose a people, gave them His law, and promised that a Savior would come. The 27 books of the New Testament tell of that Savior arriving in Jesus, the birth of the church, and the hope of all things being made new.
The Old Testament can feel distant, but it is not a different story with a different God. It is the first half of the same story, and Jesus Himself treated every word of it as the Word of God.

5.2 - Which shelf of the library would you most like to explore, and why?
Every Shelf Points to Jesus
The library has many shelves, but it has one main subject. Jesus said this to some very careful Bible readers:
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.

You can know a lot about the Bible and still miss the point. The Law shows why we need a Savior. The History books show God keeping His promises through kings who never fully kept theirs. The Poetry gives words to our longing, the Prophets point to a coming King, and the Gospels show Him.

Even Josiah could tear down idols but could not change a heart, and after he died the nation drifted again. Jeremiah, a prophet who began his ministry in Josiah's day, carried this promise from God: "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33). Jesus came to keep that promise. He is the King Josiah could not be. Through Him, God writes His Word on your heart, not as a test you must pass, but as a gift of grace.
The Bible Is "Your Very Life"

Many scholars believe the scroll found in the temple was the book of Deuteronomy, on the very first shelf of the library. One of its most famous passages sounds a lot like the way Scripture remembers Josiah:

Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart.

Josiah turned to the LORD "with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might." He did not only find the book. He let it find him. This is the Shema, which Jesus called the greatest commandment, and you met it in Lesson 1. Now you know where it lives: Deuteronomy, in the Law, on the first shelf. That is what a map does.
This is not a book to study once and set aside. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses said it plainly:
For it is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess.
Jesus said the same in the wilderness: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4).

A Word on Translations

Some translations, like the ESV and NASB, lean toward word-for-word accuracy, which helps with careful study. Others, like the NIV and NLT, lean toward thought-for-thought clarity, which helps with steady reading.

Unless noted, quotations in this course are from the ESV. Now and then a lesson uses another faithful translation on purpose, when its wording carries a key idea, and labels it. The best translation is the one you will actually open.
This Week's Practice

This week, take a book off three different shelves. Read one chapter from the Law, one from Poetry and Wisdom, and one from the Gospels. Try Deuteronomy 6, Psalm 23, and Luke 24. You will meet the Shema, the Shepherd, and the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures. As you read each chapter, ask one simple question: How does this point me to Jesus?
Lesson 5 Review

You now have the map. The Bible is a library of 66 books arranged in sections: Law, History, Poetry and Wisdom, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, Letters, and Revelation. The Old Testament promises, and the New Testament shows God keeping every promise in Jesus. Like Josiah, you do not have to leave God's Word lost in the house. God's Word is a library to open, not a book to lose on a shelf, and every shelf points to Jesus.
In the next lesson, you will take the road trip through the one big story that ties the whole library together.
